FFS. My mum was treated incredulously for being a doctoral candidate ('you're not one of the young men's wives?!') by the Oxford Department of Materials ... in 1974. You'd wish they'd have changed a little since then, but seems not:
Does it count as Stockholm syndrome that I've spent so long reading medieval clerics that I've genuinely started using 'lesbian' and 'deviant' as synonyms?

I am so proud of my third-year students as they come through their final exams.

Doctoring up here too. I earned my doctorate and still get told my research is 'made up' (there were no interesting women, let alone lesbians, in the past), that dyslexics can't do English, that women aren't experts. Fuck that.

My parents and older brother all have doctorates. When I got mine, my younger brother asked, shocked 'but you won't *use* it will you?' He couldn't explain why mine would be so much less worth using that my father's or brother's, which he never questioned.
You are very kind! Onwards and upwards to the doctorate!
I was in an abusive relationship, aged 22. In desperation to get away, I applied for a Masters and put down in the subject I'd got my highest grades in at undergrad - medieval literature.

Retweeting that last very niche Anglo-Catholic joke, I remembered that a few months ago I was really concerned how a tiny Anglican congregation in rural Yorkshire would feel about two lesbian mums. Now of course I realise it was us saying 'trespasses' not 'sins' that mattered.
Yay! Anne Lister is officially a lesbian again. Now so long as she's also not an entrepreneur, I'm happy.

WTF? reports 'schoolboys died in cliff fall with father'. Erm, no, their father drugged them and their mother, stabbed her more than 60 times, and chucked himself and his children off a cliff. It was not an accident.

If you're vain I am too! I *finally* got a good haircut today, over a year after moving away from my lovely hairdresser. A year of 'no, really, *shorter* ... no, please don't "soften" my face with those long bits ... no, I am not worried it will look a bit "harsh".
Owls are the best! When we first moved to Yorkshire my partner drew back the curtains to see a very cross owl six on the window ledge, annoyed to be disturbed. :D Now they nest in our trees.

Age 11, two of my female teachers lived together. 1996, and I was dead lucky to go to that school as we got proper LGB(no T that I remember!) sex education, which wasn't legal in state schools at the time.
Today's post: lesbian literature and the erotics of the outdoors, plus some snarking at male writers who think gay men did everything first.

Plus, this chosen academic 'family' contrasts pointedly with those members of my actual family, whose first concern with my publication record including terms like 'queer' is 'but ... do you worry your colleagues may realise you're a lesbian'? :D

YY, this! Did my undergrad there and then taught there, and IMO one of the biggest negative influences on students is the external pressure to 'look cultured' or 'look clever' rather than to be themselves. They've earned the right to be there already - no need to prove it again.
I remember my lecturers introducing me to medieval literature. Never thought I'd be the one another set of medievalists are remembering, but beyond delighted to find it's so. #tinyjoys #piersplowman.

Delighted to say it's my first day as an funded postdoctoral fellow. Here's a link to my project: Women's Reproductive Dysfunctions: Miscarriage, Abortion, Stillbirth and Infertility in Medieval England.

I wrote this post for #pregnancyloss awareness week. I'm working on recovering histories of loss, and giving us a new perspective on the emotions of loss and grieving. Here's a father in 1534 remembering his stillborn son:
Sharing this again for #pregnancyloss awareness week. I think it's so important to challenge the myth that grieving loss is something we only do nowadays (which cuts us off from history).

This is just so deeply cathartic for me. A very confident, going-places-academically fellow student shamed me for not knowing who Bloom was as an undergrad, and I have been assuming he was Ye Great Untouchable Authority ever since.

As someone who's had to read Mary's response to Gabriel announcing she'll have a baby ('how can this be, seeing I know not a man') to a packed church while my lesbian partner tries to stop my daughter yelling 'mummy!', I am gobsmacked you think Christmas isn't queer.

(Eg., I've winced when someone paraphrased my very careful use of language around sexuality in a certain way - I was really worried it made me look like a bigot, and the person tweeting obviously wasn't aware of that as a possible interpretation.)

YY. The first openly gay man I met (at university) was from NE and had absolutely terrifying stories. I really hate the rhetoric of 'queer is so inclusive now it's no longer offensive,' because it suggests those of us who got hurt are fossils.

I agree with this. I was single w/o kids when I moved for my first postdoc and it was horrifically lonely for a year; I moved again with my partner and daughter and honestly, it was much easier, because I had them.

I'd ask them to come to my (small c) church. I keep seeing this posed as a generational conflict. We have an elderly congregation and a vicar near retirement age; they've welcomed two lesbian mums with open arms and made us feel we have a family.

I graduated in summer 2014; I still haven't and probably won't (I have a couple of unrelated articles out, and a book forthcoming this year). I mention it because it was the right decision for me and I'd have been quicker with the forthcoming book if I'd realised sooner!

Well, and also, some of us write PhDs that represent a whole lot of learning, but are just ... not very good. Right? My thesis was not that great. I trust the examiners who passed it, but I am open-eyed. My book is much, much better. So the learning experience worked.
:D Ha, I can relate to that! I came across some of my undergrad essays the other month, and ... oooh, ouch!

Yes! They love them. When we first moved to our current home the garden was very overgrown with dandelions and we were overwhelmed with goldfinches doing this.

One of the things I was most frightened about before I had my baby was that I'd end up hurting her; people really need to stop meeting that fear with glib 'oh, if the baby's happy you will be happy' comments.

It's International Day Against Homophobia, Transphobia and Biphobia. Here are my selfish hopes for the future. No one: - asking who my child's 'real' mum is - calling my partner a man to her face - telling me I am basically a bad copy of a dad. Thanks all. #IDAHOBIT.
Oh, no! And demolishing Green's. I loved that place. I wrote half my MSt dissertation there.
I mainly just want to attend this summer school, of course.
Yes, it's the plebs who don't own cars/houses/large country estates who've really been showing us all up in this pandemic, I do find.

And how did I write a whole book on female same-sex desire and no one told me about Lady Lechery getting it on with Mary Magdalene? It's totally my own fault, but I feel cheated by the entire medievalist drama community right now.

This caught my eye, because I thought feminists still discussed this sort of thing! I do, anyway. I am also a radfem lesbian. I don't wear makeup much, but do wear heels and have the same dilemma on occasion.

Ducking out of #RemoteRetreat session 3 a fraction early because I got paid (yay!) and can therefore afford to shop. Hope you all had a good session!
It's not 'the UK' any more than the people who shot George Floyd are 'the US'. Which is to say, it *is* the UK, and many of us in the UK are furious and ashamed about it.

Not surprised some women think it's legally required. I got married in 2010 and was told by my bank I was legally required to change my name and title.

I had no funding for my MA; I had funding for my PhD. a) During my MA I heard the 'how dare you not do well at your studies when you've taken funding from another deserving candidate' line often; I really hate it. No one said to to me during my PhD, though. 1/2
I finished my book index today, and the radical feminist in me is quietly pleased with that the entry 'male bodies' reads 'see also castration'.

OMG yes. I *loved* my first job post-doc, and it was wonderful and taught me so much - and it was also 26 months of a heavy teaching load. I got my current fellowship because I was a *month* within a five years post PhD limit (and only because they counted to graduation not viva)

I can relate. I've had some fertility treatment (not IVF) and my partner gave birth to our daughter. So I don't know how hard carrying a pregnancy to term is, or recovering from labour, but I think the silence around compromised fertility is very damaging.

In my first year lecturing I had a hellish Thursday where I lectured from 9am to 1am straight, and I lost my voice completely. I was allowed to postpone because I literally couldn't talk, but otherwise 'you'd have had to push through'. Not sensible advice.
I just came across the anecdote that, when his son died at one year old, Francois II of Brittany made a donation of the baby's weight in gold in his memory. I find this very poignant.

I've repeatedly been asked to teach courses with no access at all - not even a library card. I am angry about that. I know about grad students who're cut off from libraries when their funding ends, and that also seems needlessly unfair.
Ooh, yes! The second-last holiday I went on, I went to the Lakes with my PhD mates just before we got our degrees. My car broke down on the way up, and I got called to an interview at the same time.

I cried in a prof's office in my MA; the prof declared triumphantly, 'see, you're easily upset!' I don't mind that memory (it says more about him than me). I do mind the memories of all the times I was so busy making sure I didn't cry, I also didn't ask for help.
One of the nastiest experiences I had in academia was at the end of my PhD. I'd handed in my thesis and passed my viva, and I'd carefully worked through my examiners' corrections. 1/-

My supervisor had printed out parts of my thesis, and suggested we look at the print out. None of the lines ended in the same places as my notes; I'd lost all of my mark-up for navigating. (Note: this is tricky for dyslexics). I went to pieces. 7/-

It didn't even occur to me to mention the £100 train, the fact my personal life and health were a total mess. I was about to get divorced; my GP had just prescribed me antidepressants and was quite worried about me; I had gynae issues. 11/-
I attend church regularly with my child and my partner (and we're often the youngest three people there), but it is hard to feel welcome in a church that won't marry us.

'Sky History stands against racism and hate speech of all kinds, and those several hours where we frantically retweeted a lying denial that a man covered in Nazi symbols was, in fact, covered in Nazi symbols? Just limbering up for the stand.'
Just had an email offering generous grant funding there to be applied for, by the early deadline of December 2019. This really is the year that keeps on giving.

I studied Latin from age 12 through A Level and also alongside my undergrad and postgrad degrees; for a medievalist in our generation I have a lot of training, and I am nowhere *close* to being able to translate like that.

My partner got to fully dilated and pushing before she had an emergency section - I am in awe of *everyone* who gives birth, however they do it. You are all heroines. (But yes. The pumpkin-vaginas are terrifying.)
(This is a heck of a coincidence, because I'm also a lesbian who's talked a fair bit about how my partner and I were treated during pregnancy/on labour wards! Seems I have an alter ego.)

Also a terribly sad one. UK again. When my grandmother went into labour they left her alone, and after a while my grandfather got worried and broke the rules about men in delivery rooms to go in and check on her. She had delivered a baby who had died.

My grandfather's cousin was an amazing woman. She was very dear to us and she influenced me a lot. She was a C of E nun, and she died in 2007. I remember her telling me she hoped very deeply that I would have a happy family life.
Like a lot of us, I tried very hard. I married a man who was incredibly kind. I think we both kept hoping things would somehow work out. But - for all sorts of reasons - they didn't.

Eventually, I met my partner. The #BeautifulStory implies that same-sex relationships are seductive and shallow and easy. But they're not. Ours wasn't easy at all. It's still not always easy. That's reality.
But, it was a wake-up call to realise that I was meant to be with a woman, and that was right for me in the Church.

But I find it really frightening and upsetting to think it would be so easy to go to a church and not know that the vicar performing the service, also believes I am doing something fundamentally un-Christian by being there, with my partner and my child.

I designed and delivered multiple lecture courses at undergrad and postgrad level without any formal training/oversight beyond a weekend 'boot camp' designed at teaching PhD students how to teach classes.

(And don't get me started on the issue of having - perfectly legally - changed name mid-way through. I am still hitting issues because my name has changed, and the thought of how hard it must be for non- UK citizens makes me shiver. It should not be this this stupidly unclear.)

Yes, indeed! I was a student when people in charge of me decided - and I am still angry about it - to pressure me to waive confidentiality and contact my parents. It was very damaging. It could have been so, so much worse.

It is. At the time it set me up for physical and sexual abuse. It's something I feel very strongly about. I'm sure it had a lot to do with me going back into the closet and not coming out again until I was nearly 30. I really can't say what a violation of trust it is.

In my third year of university, I was going through a bad time. My director of studies judged (and probably rightly) that I was a danger to myself and others. He had arranged for me to see a counsellor, but as he became more concerned, he decided to set aside confidentiality.
I was told I had to go back to live with my parents. It was incredibly frightening. I had not come out to my director of studies; I did not feel able to explain to him why I felt so frightened.

This, plus the stupidity of Oxford therefore choosing to award degrees that sound like something dodgy. I have an Oxford MSt, and it arouses quite a lot of scepticism from people who think it's a fake degree. They do it because they've used MA Oxon already.

Yes, it's really stupid. I got to use a computer for my exams, but it should be routine for everyone. My signature is so crappy I have a note lodged with my bank saying that it is inconsistent and they need to do security questions instead.
